Entertainment.title: Who is in Celebrity Traitors? From Michael Sheen to Maya Jama
Entertainment.text:
Celebrity Traitors returns next week for a second round of deception and amateur detective work.

Hosted by Claudia Winkleman, the Traitors castle will welcome 21 new celebrities on Thursday, as a group of famous "faithfuls" attempts to work out which among them are - and perhaps, always have been - "traitors", secretly murdering contestants each night.

Last year's show provided Bafta's most memorable TV moment - an award voted for by the British public - when traitor Alan Carr broke down in tears at the end of the final having bluffed his way to a win by hiding in plain sight.

Let's have a stab in the dark, then, at who might follow in Jonathan Ross's footsteps as this year's "big dog", and who, like singer Cat Burns, could fly under the radar?

If Carr was the star of last year's show, then perhaps his fellow TV funnymen could be the ones to watch this time around.

Naturally good readers of a room and skilled at misdirection, comedians can inject some comic relief into those tense roundtable moments.

It worked for Carr, who was considered to be less of a threat and more out of his depth by the other sleuths.

This time around, stand-up star Joe Lycett, 38, is one of the leading candidates for the role of class clown. Known for his quick wit and political stunts, Lycett told the BBC he asked Carr for advice on "how to spot a rotten little traitor like you".

Last year's winner replied: "Just anyone that's sweating and giggling."

With his brightly coloured outfits, Lycett will bring some glamour to the castle, if and when he's not donning the famous dark cloak.

"There's a lot of variety and silly stuff that I might not get to wear at all if I end up doing a Paloma," he noted, with reference to Paloma Faith, who was brutally killed off early doors last year by her supposed friend, Carr.

If laughing all the way to the winning line is to work again, then it's hard to look beyond James Acaster.

Anyone who has seen his Netflix special Repertoire or heard his podcast Off Menu will know his deadpan, absurdist humour and whimsical flights of fancy could make it difficult to tell whether he is telling the truth or not.

A "huge fan" of the show since the first non-celebrity edition in 2022, Acaster, 41, said he would prefer to be a faithful as he wasn't good at lying - though Carr did previously say something similar...

Romesh Ranganathan's dry humour and wry presenting style saw him succeed Anne Robinson as the host of The Weakest Link revival in 2021. Could it help him to become a more believable traitor or faithful?

The former maths teacher and now comedy podcaster, 48, blamed his youngest son, who was "desperate for me to come on", for his reluctant participation this year.

One of his best friends on the comedy circuit, Parenting Hell podcaster Rob Beckett, is another of this year's funniest contestants.

A decade's worth of friendship with the 8 Out of 10 Cats and Mock the Week panellist could count for nothing in the castle, Ranganathan said. He believes Beckett, 40, is "just as easily going to be on my side as he is going to twist the knife in my back given the opportunity".

One of the nation's other most celebrated comics, Miranda Hart will no doubt be a big personality among the group.

In her self-titled sitcom, she starred as an awkward, accident-prone shopkeeper. Her apparent clumsiness and warm, self-deprecating persona might make her seem more trustworthy (rightly or wrongly).

After a spell of ill-health, Hart, 53, hopes "the joy of mucking about on television again will hopefully outweigh some of the challenges".

Irish comedian Joanne McNally, 43, could also be the joker of the pack this year. Her popular podcast My Therapist Ghosted Me is full of gossip, oversharing and comic bickering - music to the ears of the Traitors producers, no doubt.

Her stand-up is confessional and brutally honest. But honesty gets you nowhere in this game - or does it?

The "Big Dog Theory" was a piece of gameplay logic proposed by ex-rugby union star Joe Marler during roundtable discussions last year.

His reasoning was that one of the most famous contestants, AKA the big dogs, would have been chosen as a traitor to cause mass confusion (and, presumably, strong viewing figures).

Marler wondered out loud whether the big dog traitor in question was Sir Stephen Fry (no) or Jonathan Ross (yes).

For the new series, a glut of huge names and personalities from across the worlds of film, TV, music, modelling and broadcasting have also been selected.

Michael Sheen, the award-winning Welsh actor and campaigner, is perhaps the biggest dog in the fight, so will come under real scrutiny.

Sheen, 57, is acclaimed for his ability to convincingly portray a range of different personalities on screen, from Tony Blair to Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor via Brian Clough.

But in real life, he's seen more as a loveable golden retriever than a Rottweiler, despite his success. Which version of him we shall see on the show remains to be seen.

Fellow big screen charmer Richard E. Grant, 69, who starred in films such as Withnail and I, may also leave some of the less well-known celebrities star-struck at first, as might American-British supermodel/actress Jerry Hall.

Hall, 70, shares four children with ex-partner Mick Jagger and has also been married to media mogul Rupert Murdoch.

Love Island presenter Maya Jama, 32, and University Challenge host, journalist and YouTuber Amol Rajan are also powerhouses in the world of broadcasting.

Speaking ahead of the show, 43-year-old Rajan, who is in it to win it, said : "I don't want to go in there and at round table number one be Mr Forensic Investigator!

"However, I do interview politicians for a living, and I really have to pursue answers to questions."

He's conscious of putting "a target" on his back too soon, so plans to form alliances.

"To begin with, I want to try and make friends and keep my head down," he added.

EastEnders hardman turned hard-hitting documentarian Ross Kemp, 62, might prove popular once the tasks get physical.

And we don't know yet whether to expect the soppy You're Beautiful balladeer James Blunt, 52, or the prolific (and hilarious) online troll of the same name.

Either way, if the Big Dog Theory holds true, then one of the above will surely find themselves in the traitors' turret before long.

Little Mix and solo singing star Leigh-Anne Pinnock, 34, may be a big dog in the world of pop music, but she comes across as a down-to-earth family woman these days.

Don't be fooled, though, as she has a wealth of experience of managing relationships under intense public pressure from her girl group days.

Meanwhile, another potential dark horse, Bella Ramsey, revealed they had been playing a version of The Traitors since they were 10 years old, even hosting events at home - so should be well-prepared.

Now 22, the Last of Us star, who also featured in Game of Thrones, is the youngest of this year's contestants but should not be underestimated. The Traitors castle should be a cakewalk compared with the apocalypse or the Battle of Winterfell, right?

The plan is to be "instinctive, measured, and perceptive", Ramsey said. "I will be keeping my opinions to myself until I feel it's absolutely the right time to share them."

King Kenny, a member of popular British YouTube collective Beta Squad, is known for pranks, vlogs and more recently (and briefly), boxing.

The 29-year-old will be hoping the class of 2026 has more faith in online influencers than last year, when his Beta Squadmate Niko Omilana was the first player banished from the castle.

Omilana's early exit also sparked a discussion among some critics about non-white contestants being voted off UK/US reality game shows at an early stage, and whether unconscious bias may play a role.

Mathematician and broadcaster, Hannah Fry, who co-hosts The Rest is Science podcast, could fill David Olusoga's intellectual shoes this year.

Historian Olusoga quietly made it to the final last year despite having repeatedly voted out faithfuls thinking they were traitors.

Fry, 42, said she was "here to fulfil the nerd quota" and was taking the responsibility "extremely seriously".

She added: "I would say people tend to think I'm smarter than I actually am, bluntly, and I don't think that's going to serve me particularly well as I may be seen as a bit of a threat."

If the comedians are aiming to be the next Carr, then who could be the new Cat Burns and fly under the radar all the way to the final?

US actress Myha'la, 30, who plays Harper Stern in banking bonkbuster series Industry, may be top pick.

Unlike her ruthless character on the show, she said she was more of a "kill them with kindness kind of girl rather than a blatantly bullish bulldog". She added: "All that said, I want to be a Traitor. Obviously!"

She's deliberately planned her look - clothes, hair and jewellery - to separate herself from Stern and "be seen as me and not that character".

Julie Hesmondhalgh, will be known to audiences Up North especially as Roy Cropper's wife Hayley in the soap Coronation Street, between 1998 and 2014.

Hesmondhalgh, 56, who also appeared in Broadchurch and Mr Bates vs the Post Office, won't struggle to make friends with her warm personality. But they'd be wise not to forget she is, after all, a talented and experienced actress.

Sharon Rooney, star of My Mad Fat Diary and the Barbie film, is another contestant likely to keep a low profile, which, as we've seen, can work well up to a point.

But will it trigger suspicion of the Scottish Lawyer Barbie actress, 37, eventually?

And last but not least, Sebastian Croft, star of the recent Netflix coming-of-age hit Heartstopper, rounds off our list. Younger viewers will know all about Croft, 24, already, but will the older contestants?

Some names are bigger than others right now, but as three of last year's finalists - Burns, Olusoga and Nick Mohammed - discovered, that could change quickly over the coming episodes.

The Celebrity Traitors returns to BBC One and iPlayer on Thursday, 1 October.

Entertainment.title: Before BTS and Blackpink, there was Big Bang: Now the Kings of K-pop are back
Entertainment.text:
A sea of glowing yellow crowns. Thousands of voices chanting in Korean.

An explosive surge of energy as the opening synth riffs of Fantastic Baby shatter the stadium air. Big Bang is back.

Fourteen years after their first major European shows, and after a decade marked by military service, member departures and legal scandals, the South Korean group played at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium in London on Saturday as part of their 20th anniversary world tour.

Inside the near-capacity venue, the crowd did not just watch a concert - they stepped into a significant moment in K-pop history.

As the band emerged in their trademark high-fashion, glittering outfits, the crowd danced freely, setting the tone for an evening that felt less like a routine tour stop and more like a homecoming.

For fans, it is a long-awaited reunion. But the significance of Big Bang's return extends beyond nostalgia.

Years before BTS were selling out Wembley Stadium and Blackpink were headlining Hyde Park, Big Bang were already proving Korean pop could succeed far beyond Asia.

The group filled arenas across the West, collaborated with major American artists, experimented with hip-hop and electronic music, and turned their own fashion and creative identities into part of their appeal.

Having attended their European debut at Wembley Arena in 2012, the shift in atmosphere on Saturday was striking.

Where their original UK shows were driven by a hunger to prove themselves and promote a new album, this return as a trio, comprising G-Dragon, Taeyang and Daesung, felt entirely crafted for their dedicated community.

By reworking classic tracks and cleverly remixing songs to accommodate absent members, the group relied on pyrotechnics, their signature live band and sheer stage presence rather than elaborate staging.

The result was a reunion that felt celebratory, grounded and playful.

In 2011, Big Bang became the first K-pop group to win a major Western music award when they took home the newly created Worldwide Act prize at the MTV Europe Music Awards.

When they made their European debut at Wembley Arena in December 2012, a second show was added after the first sold out in under two hours.

They were leading a pioneering generation that proved global crossover was genuinely possible.

Then in 2016, Forbes estimated Big Bang had earned $44m (£33.2m) over the previous year, making them the first K-pop act to appear on its Celebrity 100 List.

"When it comes to the global market for K-pop, there is no doubt Big Bang made a huge contribution," says Dr Haekyung Um, senior lecturer in music at the University of Liverpool.

"Earlier acts were popular within Asian markets, but Big Bang were true international stars. I would call them the Kings of K-pop, just as we call Michael Jackson the King of Pop," Um adds.

"Big Bang's success really was an early signal of how successful a K-pop stadium tour in the West could truly be."

Before Big Bang, K-pop groups were often viewed as heavily manufactured by entertainment agencies.

But music critics say Big Bang broke the mould. They wrote and produced their own songs, shaped their own streetwear image and blended genres ranging from hip-hop and R&B to trot, a traditional South Korean folk genre.

For many attending on Saturday, the show served as a direct lesson in K-pop's lineage - a chance to see "the idols' idols" perform live.

"They were different because they didn't follow the uniform K-pop cookie-cutter pretty boy phase," explains Sharon, who was visiting London from Singapore.

"They went harder on their music, a bit more hip-hop. They did what they had to do, and they are the absolute OGs for me."

The shift set them apart across Asia and helped establish the blueprint for modern self-produced acts such as BTS.

And then there is the yellow crown. At Big Bang concerts, it is impossible to miss the group's crown-shaped lightstick, known as the Bang Bong.

In early K-pop, fans supported artists by waving coloured balloons or generic glow sticks.

But seeking a distinct, permanent identity for their fandom, dubbed "VIPs", band leader G-Dragon proposed a handheld yellow crown, setting the template for custom concert merchandise.

"Fan engagement and coordinated chants have deep roots in Korean music history," explains Um. "But Big Bang helped modernise the physical technology."

The Bang Bong established a model for custom-designed fandom lightsticks and merchandise that modern K-pop groups now follow.

Outside the venue, that same fan-led energy spilled into the streets, with attendees trading handmade gifts and photo cards - a ritual that has spread to Western arena tours in recent years.

Volunteer fan groups distributed roughly 35,000 custom-printed banners across the stadium, co-ordinating a massive crowd-wide salute to be raised in unison during select performances.

Big Bang's story, however, is far from a straightforward tale of success.

South Korea requires able-bodied men to complete mandatory military service, and Big Bang's members served at different points during the group's hiatus.

Then came the scandals.

In 2017, former band member T.O.P was convicted of marijuana use, an offence heavily criminalised and socially taboo in South Korea, and received a suspended prison sentence while serving his mandatory military duty. He later formally departed from the group.

Then in 2019, the group's youngest member, Seungri, permanently retired from entertainment amid the "Burning Sun" scandal.

It was a high-profile police investigation into a Seoul nightclub of the same name which exposed a network of sex trafficking, bribery, and illicit filming involving several male K-pop stars.

South Korea's Supreme Court later upheld an 18-month prison sentence for Seungri in 2022 on charges including prostitution mediation, overseas gambling, and embezzlement.

Although the band didn't openly acknowledge the departure of two of their former members from the stage, their absence was obvious to long-time fans in the audience.

Though it did not matter to fans like Annie, who flew from New York to see the show with friends. She said Big Bang's perseverance through hardship made their music mean even more.

"Big Bang was my starter," she says. "I love how they move through the obstacles - it gives me hope. After years of hiatus, it's amazing they're coming back. They are the OGs."

The crowd erupted as the opening chant of Bang Bang Bang echoed before the band even walked out, while their iconic 2008 ballad Haru Haru produced a massive stadium-wide singalong.

The K-pop industry Big Bang helped build has changed almost beyond recognition.

Yet their return has drawn a striking mix of original second-generation fans and younger Gen Z listeners who were barely born when the group debuted.

While many veteran followers grew up alongside the band, a whole new generation discovered them through digital archives or cross-media appearances.

Gemma and her daughter Casey travelled from Edinburgh wearing handmade custom jackets.

"I found out about them through T.O.P in Squid Game and then fell down a rabbit hole," Gemma says. "I've converted so many of my friends to K-pop now. It's all about the energy."

For Korean diaspora fans, the show carried an even deeper cultural resonance.

"I got into Big Bang when their Alive EP (in 2012) was released because I felt they were quite ground-breaking," says Kevin.

"Before, I felt there was a lot of mimicking by Korean artists on what was happening in the West, but here they took full ownership of their unique identity. It's very rare in K-pop that you have a band around for 20 years, and they definitely played a part in making K-pop mainstream."

Much of this multi-generational pull is driven by archival concert footage, TV appearances, and classic music videos circulating across social media platforms like TikTok and YouTube.

"Nostalgia can be built upon something people didn't even experience personally at the time," notes Um.

"It comes through shared digital memory. YG Entertainment was early in leveraging digital platforms like YouTube, which built a lasting global fan foundation that has accumulated across two generations."

While the band refrained from directly addressing their past on stage, the emotional weight of their history peaked during the finale Still Life.

As T.O.P's unmistakable baritone echoed through the stadium via recorded vocals, a visible wave of emotion swept across the crowd.

Addressing the venue during the encore, G-Dragon appeared clearly moved, admitting they never expected their music to leave such an enduring global mark 14 years after their London debut.

As fireworks lit up the night sky, the three members linked hands and bowed deeply - a triumphant moment for the group widely credited with helping reshape modern K-pop.

Entertainment.title: Ed Sheeran concerts cancelled becuase of bad weather
Entertainment.text:
Ed Sheeran's concerts in Massachusetts on Friday and Saturday have been cancelled because of severe weather warnings in the area.

The singer had been scheduled to perform two shows at the Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, near Boston, as part of his current US tour.

The tour has been in the headlines because of a row over a decision to drop Sheeran's support act Macklemore for making pro-Palestinian comments on stage. Stadium owners including the Gillette Stadium's Robert Kraft lobbied for his removal.

A statement from the venue, external said: "Due to the severe weather warnings in place in Boston and across New England throughout the weekend and following consultation with local officials, the promoter and tour have made the difficult decision to cancel the Ed Sheeran concerts at Gillette Stadium."

It added: "The decision was made with the safety of fans, staff and everyone involved in the shows as the top priority.

"Refunds are available now at the point of purchase. Ticketholders who purchased through Ticketmaster will be automatically refunded."

Weather warnings for high winds are in force in the area until the early hours of Sunday, and officials have told drivers to minimise travel.

Sheeran was at the eye of a very different storm last week after the decision to drop Macklemore from his tour.

The decision came after the rapper made on-stage comments at earlier concerts including calling for "free Palestine" and referring to "genocide" in Gaza, as well as showing images of Gaza.

Kraft, who is Jewish, accused the US rapper of hate speech and said Macklemore would not be allowed to appear at the Gillette Stadium, the home of his New England Patriots American football team.

Sheeran said the decision to drop Macklemore was made by his promoter, not by him. The promoter said venue owners including Kraft would have refused to let the concerts take place if Macklemore was on the bill.

Macklemore's removal from the tour led Sheeran's other support and backing artists to pull out in protest, and sparked a heated debate over free speech and the role of politics in music.

Returning to the stage last weekend, Sheeran told fans he "had to take and make difficult decisions - and I am making mistakes - and I'm so, so sorry".

Entertainment.title: Jay-Z rape accuser formally withdraws allegation
Entertainment.text:
A woman who accused Jay-Z of raping her when she was 13 has formally said her allegation was untrue.

The unnamed woman filed a lawsuit in 2024 claiming she had been drugged and raped by Jay-Z, real name Shawn Carter, and Sean "Diddy" Combs at a party after the MTV Video Music Awards in 2000.

The stars denied the allegation and she dropped the lawsuit last year. Carter then sued her and her lawyers.

In a statement filed in that case on Thursday, she wrote: "Shawn 'Jay-Z' Carter never raped me. I have never met or spoken to Mr. Carter. Mr. Carter never engaged in any inappropriate conduct toward me whatsoever."

The woman, known in court documents by the pseudonym Jane Doe, also said: "My claims that Mr Carter and Mr Combs raped me while a third celebrity, [name redacted] watched are false. There is no truth to any of my claims against Mr Carter.

"I understand my false accusations have caused Mr Carter immense pain, suffering, and damage that can never be fully undone."

Carter had vehemently denied the accusations, saying they were a "blackmail attempt" and describing them as "frivolous, fictitious and appalling allegations".

When the accuser dropped her case in February 2025, the rapper, who is married to singer Beyoncé, said: "The trauma that my wife, my children, loved ones and I have endured can never be dismissed."

The woman, from Alabama, has now been removed from Carter's lawsuit.

She said she had not received any money from the rap superstar or anyone acting on his behalf, and had not been paid to make her latest declaration.

The rapper is still suing the woman's former lawyers, led by Tony Buzbee.

In a statement to Rolling Stone, external, which first reported Jane Doe's new declaration, Buzbee said he had not seen it.

He said: "We have multiple lawyers (at least four) who dealt with Ms Doe long before she met me. She gave the exact same story to each. If for some reason now she is claiming she lied to us and the court, that's new information."

When Carter filed his lawsuit against the woman and her lawyers in February 2025, Buzbee claimed at the time that Carter's investigators had "repeatedly harassed, threatened and harangued this poor woman for weeks, trying to intimidate her and make her recant her story".

In her new declaration, the woman said: "I never received any threat from Mr Carter or anyone acting on his behalf."

Entertainment.title: U2 celebrate 50th anniversary at the school where they formed
Entertainment.text:
Exactly 50 years after they formed, U2 returned to Dublin to play a gig at the school where they met.

"We've escaped from the lab," declared Bono, as the quartet took to a stage in the playground. "How's the experiment working for you?"

The pupils of Mount Temple Comprehensive may not have been born when U2 were the world’s biggest band, but they gave them a hero's welcome, waving signs that said, "I love U2", "It's a beautiful day - no school", and, "Bono, my mum says hi!"

The group treated them to a career-spanning set that included hits like I Will Follow, Vertigo and With Or Without You, as well as their latest single, Silencio.

As they played, teachers pulled down pupils who’d climbed on their classmates' shoulders, before getting swept up in the moment and dancing along themselves.

As he looked out from the same stage where U2 made their debut in 1976, Bono became emotional.

"Thanks for, er… Yeah... I didn't… Wow," said the frontman, temporarily lost for words.

The U2 story began in those same halls and corridors five decades ago, when 14-year-old Larry Mullen Jr pinned a handwritten note to the school noticeboard.

"Drummer seeks musicians to form band."

Auditions were held a couple of days later, on 25 September, 1976, in Larry's parents' kitchen.

Among the hopeful "misfits", as their school-friend Frank Kearns called them, were Bono, The Edge and Adam Clayton – who arrived wearing a full-length Afghan coat.

Initially called Feedback, and then The Hype, they conquered the world as U2, transforming themselves from a scrappy punk outfit into stadium-conquering rock titans, whose big ideas and big anthems attracted millions of admirers, and almost as many detractors.

Speaking to BBC News, Mullen confessed the infamous wanted advert had been his father's idea all along.

"I'd been playing on my own, in my house, and my dad was pretty frustrated," he says.

"I wasn't very good at many things, and playing the drums was included in that. So I think he, out of frustration, said I should try and play with other people."

"And unfortunately," adds Bono, "he got the three of us."

Bono, then known as Paul Hewson, had actually been tempted to skip the audition. He was two years older, and concerned about looking out of place.

"I wouldn't be hanging out with second years, and particularly really good-looking ones," he says.

Eventually, his friend Reggie Manuel persuaded him to attend, even giving him a lift on his rickety old motorbike.

"I can tell myself it was a Harley Davidson," the singer jokes, "but really it was a Yamaha DX100."

The first band practice didn't exactly show promise.

There was more talking than playing. Clayton, a bassist who couldn't play bass, was selected on account of having "the best hair". And Bono, who wanted to be the guitarist, didn't bring a guitar.

"I was never any good with gear," he reflects. "Carrying it, unpacking it, that kind of thing."

Even so, there were signs the band would attract an adoring legion of fans. Half-way through the rehearsal, a group of screaming girls tried to climb the garden wall.

For Clayton, that was the moment that sealed the deal.

"Larry already had a fan club, and we thought, 'Well, if he's got a fan club, that looks pretty good to us. Maybe if we hang out with this guy, it might stretch a little further'."

Mullen, forever the band's stoic moral compass, was not impressed by the invasion.

"As I recall, Larry Mullen took a hose to the fans," laughs Bono.

"I don't know what possessed me," the drummer grimaces, while trying to insist the hosing "was an act of kindness and love because it was a hot day".

"They enjoyed it," he protests. "It was playful."

Bono jumps in to save his friend's embarrassment…. Well, kind of.

"It's been the story of our lives ever since. He doesn't even want to have fans, but we quite like them."

From that kitchen in Rosemount Avenue, U2 became the world's biggest rock band.

Anthems like With Or Without You, One and Beautiful Day have always sounded majestic yet personal; powered by The Edge's cascading guitar tone and Bono's lyrics which, for all their proselytising, remain grounded in a belief in humanity.

They made a stylistic swerve in the 1990s, embracing electronics, dance music and irony on the albums Achtung Baby, Zooropa and Pop.

Along the way, they reinvented stadium concerts with the Zoo TV tour, whose stage was crammed full of multimedia screens and satellite feeds, while Bono made nightly prank calls to the White House.

The Edge, real name Dave Evans, puts their longevity down to a lack of formal training.

"It's been a guiding light, in some ways, the limitations of the band," he explains.

"We're in this place where, musically, we never know what's about to happen. It can fall apart or it can become something extraordinary.

"And that's the beauty of U2.”

Back on stage at Mount Temple, Bono paid tribute to his alma matter for allowing the band to flourish.

The support of teachers allowed them to realise that “maybe all we needed was around us, just under our feet,” he said.

And he dedicated the performance to school councillor Jack Heaslip, who later became a “travelling pastor” on the band’s tours, before his death from motor neurone disease in 2015.

U2 then closed their set with an orchestral arrangement of One, assisted by students from Ireland's Music Generation education programme, which they helped fund and establish 15 years ago.

A few hours earlier, the band announced their 16th studio album, Carnaval de Luz, which will be released in November.

It's a companion piece to February's angry, impassioned EP, Days of Ash, which tackled headlines about ICE killings in America, the war in Ukraine and the Israel-Palestine conflict.

That was followed by the more sedate Easter Lily EP in April; with Carnaval de Luz rounding off the story.

The Edge described it as "a messy, provocative, sacred collection of songs", while Bono promised "loud guitars, deep bass [and] ecstatic rhythms."

Closing out the album's 12 tracks is Torn, a song co-written by Dolly Parton, which was the country icon's final recorded performance before her death last month.

In a press release, the track was described as "a tender country song detailing broken family ties, that holds wider resonances".

BBC News will run an interview about that song, and the rest of the album, in the coming weeks.

Entertainment.title: BBC Radio 2 presenter Owain Wyn Evans to cycle UK for Children In Need
Entertainment.text:
Radio presenter Owain Wyn Evans will cycle through all four UK nations to raise money for BBC Children in Need.

The Welsh host of BBC Radio 2's Early Breakfast Show will travel almost 400 miles, setting off from Glasgow and finishing in Cardiff.

The five-day challenge will start on Monday, 9 November, and finish on Friday, 13 November - when the fundraiser will be broadcast.

The only member of the annual TV fundraiser's hosting team for 2026 to be revealed so far is fellow Welsh presenter, One Show host Alex Jones.

The BBC said Evans' challenge would be the "greatest ever distance" covered in a Radio 2 endeavour for the charity.

Evans, who is originally from Ammanford, Carmarthenshire, said: "When I said yes to this challenge, I knew it would push me well outside my comfort zone.

"It's going to be tough, demanding and probably a little daunting at times, but I'm ready to give it absolutely everything I've got."

Entertainment.title: The Lost Children of Tuam: Liam Neeson involved in new movie revealing story behind babies discovery
Entertainment.text:
The story of the amateur historian whose research helped uncover the Tuam babies scandal is being brought to the big screen, with the help of actor Liam Neeson.

The Bon Secours Mother and Baby Home institution for unmarried mothers and their children was in operation from 1925 until 1961.

It came to international attention in 2014, after local historian Catherine Corless discovered there were 796 death certificates for children and babies who died there, but no burial records.

A 2017 article in the New York Times, external about Corless' journey left Neeson in a "quiet rage", he told RTÉ's Late Late Show, external, prompting him to use his standing in the film industry to bring the story to life, and be a co-producer.

"I thought if my standing in the film business is anything at all I'd love this to become a film so more people could see it and we could share this atrocity," Neeson said.

"The way the film is done, it's just true to life," Corless told BBC Radio Ulster's Good Morning Ulster programme, describing it as "fantastic".

Corless said the film's director, Frank Berry, "really wanted" the film "to be true and they stuck to the truth".

"It shows the diversity between people in power and ordinary people like myself struggling to get a story out there that I knew was true, I had all the evidence," she said.

A team is currently excavating the site of the former institution. In June, it was reported that they had found a further eight sets of infant remains, bringing the total number recovered to 77.

"I really had to fight for it to come to this stage, not for the film exactly, also the excavation in Tuam is going ahead and the exhumation. I fought years with the denial from authorities that anything wrong happened," Corless said.

"It's something I had to keep working on and that's portrayed very, very well in the film."

Entertainment.title: Middlesbrough Turner Prize exhibition 'a prestigious opportunity'
Entertainment.text:
Turner Prize nominated artworks are going on display at a gallery in what its director has called a "prestigious opportunity".

Work by four artists in the running for the prize - Simeon Barclay, Kira Freije, Marguerite Humeau and Tanoa Sasraku - will go on display at Teesside University's Middlesbrough Institute of Modern Art (MIMA) from 26 September.

Dr Laura Sillars, director of MIMA and dean of culture and creativity at the niversity, said of the exhibition: "While it's here, at a certain level, we are the centre of the creative universe."

The Turner Prize is awarded each year to a British artist for an outstanding exhibition or other presentation of their work.

Middlesbrough Mayor Chris Cooke said the exhibition, which includes works of mixed media, sculpture and spoken word, would provide residents with an "incredible opportunity" to see cutting-edge art in their home town".

He said: "I hope it inspires our young people to dream about what's possible.

"Why shouldn't it be them in a few years' time?

"Hosting the Turner Prize gives us a chance to show off what we have to offer to people across the country."

Established in 1984 and named after English Romantic painter Joseph Mallord William Turner, the prize is one of the most prestigious awards for visual arts.

The winner, who will be announced on 10 December, will be awarded £25,000, with £10,000 given to the other shortlisted artists.

Entertainment.title: Catherine Zeta-Jones bases Kill Jackie role on people she knows
Entertainment.text:
Actor Catherine Zeta-Jones says she based her performance in the new series Kill Jackie on people she knows in Wales.

The Mumbles star plays Jackie Price, a former cocaine dealer who is being targeted by hitmen, in a new series for Prime.

It is the first time she has played a role using her Swansea accent, external and the first time she has filmed a drama in Wales.

"I played on people I know in Wales, people who are comedic and the accent makes it funny and real and true, but the character comes from a tough side of Swansea, which we do have as well," she said.

The series is based on a book called The Price You Pay, set in the US, and the central character is a man called Jack.

Zeta-Jones said they "flipped it" for her to be a woman with all the quirkiness and craziness that Jack had in the book.

She said: "I told my creative team, I want to play her Welsh. And they went OK.

"For many reasons. One, I've never played real Welsh Swansea ever, never shot in Wales and I think it would ground me in her character and add nuances that I would know," she told Lucy Owen on BBC Radio Wales.

"I'm so glad I did it because she's such a great character and I just wanted her to be Welsh."

Zeta-Jones, also an executive producer on the series, said she had an idea for one scene to use a song by Welsh singing legend Tom Jones, and have him help save the day.

She said: "Jackie has installed this high-tech security system behind these Andy Warhol style prints of Tom Jones. They lift up and out come very dangerous machine-guns that do the bad guys in.

"That was my contribution to the scene."

Catherine said she did not know if Jones realised he had such a crucial role and said she needed to text him to tell him about it.

"I think because I'm playing such a badass, I think he's going to love that we used his song in that particular moment in the show," she said.

Zeta-Jones has been praised by fans for using her Welsh accent in the thriller, which begins on 2 October.

One fan said they loved hearing the "queen of Wales sounding Welsh".

She has previously spoken about her strong connection to Wales, adding in her heart she "never really left".

One fan commented on an Instagram post of the trailer, saying: "Her Welsh is out and I love it, can't wait".

Speaking on BBC Woman's Hour, Zeta-Jones said she "could not believe" how many of her fans noticed the use of her accent and that it had made her "very happy".

The Hollywood actress also revisited comments she made recently about the term "nepo baby", which she said was a "horrific" phrase.

During the interview, she said her husband Michael Douglas - son of Hollywood legend Kirk Douglas - was "the ultimate nepo baby".

She also said her children Dylan and Carys had dealt with the "intense attention thrown on them profoundly well".

Despite her Welsh pride, Zeta-Jones has also revealed that she turned down an appearance on Welcome To Wrexham, alongside fellow Hollywood stars Ryan Reynolds and Rob Mac.

In an interview with Heart Radio she said she was asked several times to feature in the documentary series.

"It's really hard to explain to Americans that I'm from Swansea and I was brought up with Swansea City. My uncle Bobby was director of the Swans when John Toshack took us to the premiership.

"I was in the front seat of the parade. I have been a lifelong Swansea city fan. I can't go to Wrexham. I can't even go to Wrexham to tell them how much I love Swansea. I think they would throw bricks at me in the street," she joked.

Entertainment.title: Media outlets banned by Trump resume White House coverage after judge's order
Entertainment.text:
Regular US television coverage resumed on Friday after the White House was forced to lift its ban of news outlets and readmit journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico.

A federal judge had ruled on Thursday that the ban was likely unconstitutional and the administration had to let them back in, at least for now. Trump had barred them for what he called "fake news".

After the ruling on Thursday, the White House still denied entry to some CNN and MS NOW reporters assigned to cover arrivals for a state dinner for Chinese leader Xi Jinping.

But on Friday, White House officials allowed reporters entry and coverage went back to normal for the last day of Xi's visit with Trump in Washington.

Four television networks that have a daily rotation of White House coverage along with CNN - ABC, CBS, Fox News and NBC - had paused their broadcasts of the president in solidarity with the banned outlets.

Despite the judge's ruling, CNN said that about an hour before Xi was scheduled to arrive for the dinner, the White House said it could cover the event only with a photojournalist and audio technician, but not a team that included a reporter and producer.

MS NOW White House reporter Laura Barron-Lopez said she was told by White House staff that she could not be let in, and to contact the White House communications director.

The BBC has contacted the White House for comment.

A White House communications account posted on X that "contrary to what the Fake News wants you to believe, they don't just get to have free rein into every part of the White House, every event, and every press call".

The incident was the latest in a series of events on Thursday surrounding the ban on some media outlets at the White House.

Despite the overnight ruling, CNN, Politico and MS NOW all reported being denied entry to the White House on Thursday morning, prompting a request for an emergency court hearing.

In response, the director of White House Operations said in a court filing that the press passes and confiscated badges had been restored by 09:45 local time (13:45 GMT).

Shortly afterwards, all three outlets said they were allowed back in.

Entertainment.title: White House television pool resumes after banned news outlets regain access
Entertainment.text:
The primary White House television pool has resumed filming administration events after a court ruling temporarily overturned a Trump administration ban on CNN a day earlier.

In an unprecedented move, the pool – which also includes NBC, ABC, CBS and Fox News – ceased recording and transmitting White House footage on Monday, in solidarity with CNN, MS Now and Politico, which had been banned by Trump from the building over what he said was “their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS.”

The decision meant that, for much of this week, there was no high-quality pool footage of White House events and the president’s movements, though some smaller outlets attempted to provide coverage.

With the pool still inactive on Thursday afternoon, that meant that a significant presidential event, a summit with Xi Jinping, China’s president, did not receive video coverage on the leading television networks. ABC had been listed as the TV pooler for the day, but held off until the network received assurances that CNN would be let back into the pool.

Tensions between the media and the administration were further exacerbated on Thursday evening when journalists for CNN and MS Now were denied access to the White House state dinner in honor of Xi. The journalists were blocked despite a ruling earlier in the day from a federal judge who granted a request by CNN, MS Now and Politico to force the White House to restore their access for the next two weeks while the case plays out.

Although television networks remain apprehensive, a producer for CBS News confirmed that the network would be serving as the TV pooler for the day as scheduled, according to an internal note obtained by the Guardian.

“The plan is to return covering the President in a normal capacity with a full crew,” the note read, with the pool covering Trump and Xi arriving at the South Portico for tea and a tour of the National Archives.

Pamela Brown, a CNN anchor, told viewers on Friday morning: “CNN’s access to the White House has been restored, and the TV pool appears to be functioning as normal.”

The resumption ends – for now – an extraordinary standoff between the US’s biggest media companies and the Trump administration that led to an effective TV blackout of coverage of the president during the United Nations general assembly.

For decades, the five networks have shared the cost and responsibility of providing footage of the president that is carried by news outlets worldwide.

Pool subscribers had originally received a note on Monday from Fox News Washington bureau chief Bryan Boughton, who is now serving as the TV pool chair, saying that it would cease operations. “This follows the White House’s position preventing CNN from fulfilling its assigned pool duties,” he wrote in a memo. “There will be no replacement pool put in place.”

In an unprecedented move, the pool – which also includes NBC, ABC, CBS and Fox News – ceased recording and transmitting White House footage...

Entertainment.title: Tomi Adeyemi on the film of her hit novel Children of Blood and Bone: ‘I don’t plan to watch it’
Entertainment.text:
There is a photograph of Tomi Adeyemi staring out from the cover of her new novel, The Siren. It is an arresting image: her face fills the frame, unsoftened by a smile, her piercing gaze fixed directly on the viewer. “It’s terrifying – like the Mona Lisa, staring at you everywhere,” she says, laughing.

Using an author portrait on the cover of a novel is highly unusual, and a decision that Adeyemi says is a statement of ownership. After 12 years spent inside the world of Children of Blood and Bone – the first book in the YA trilogy that made her a literary star and its film adaptation which has become a source of profound distress – Adeyemi wanted this book to belong unmistakably to her.

“It was an intense choice, and I think it’s because I needed people to see me in this one,” she says. “I’ve had so much success, but it was also done in a way where so many people’s interpretations were put on to who I was.”

The recent public fallout from the forthcoming film adaptation may have drawn attention, but the 33-year-old Nigerian American author had already spent much of her adult life being watched. Children of Blood and Bone, her 2018 debut, became a publishing phenomenon, netting a major seven-figure deal and debuting at No 1 on the New York Times young adult bestseller list. Its story of Zélie, a young woman fighting to restore magic to the kingdom of Orïsha, was inspired by West African mythology and offered something Adeyemi had craved as a child: a dark-skinned Black girl at the centre of an epic fantasy.

The success brought its own mythology. Adeyemi was not merely a successful young writer; she became, she feels, a symbol of what the next generation of Black YA literature might be, something she felt the weight of acutely.

“I felt pressure to be the perfect dark-skinned Black girl, to be ‘Oprah good’,” she says. “This was the biggest YA book deal in history, not just for a female or Black author. And so few of us are given a shot at all, so for the last 12 years there’s been this sense of carrying everyone.”

Readers would tell her what the book had meant to their children. “You have no idea what this did for me,” they would say. Such responses were moving, but also difficult to know what to do with.

Now, with The Siren, Adeyemi has moved from epic fantasy to something more contemporary. The standalone novel follows Emery, a Black student arriving at Dartmouth College determined to leave her troubled past behind. She is drawn into a mysterious sorority of “Sirens” and desperate to fit in. In some ways, Adeyemi says, the book is deeply personal. “[Emery] is my inner teen,” Adeyemi says. “I just want to give her a hug.”

She may have found success, but in the beginning Adeyemi’s career never looked certain. She wrote her first story at five – a Parent Trap fan fiction because, she says, she “wanted a twin and a horse”. She then spent years trying not to become a writer. Her parents had moved to Chicago from Nigeria in their early 20s, and Adeyemi grew up with the ethos of relentless achievement that often comes with first-generation immigrants – one that does not take kindly to creative pursuits. She considered medicine, investment banking and consulting, but kept coming back to writing. “Being called to be an artist is terrifying,” she says. “It’s not a logical choice.”

After studying English at Harvard, Adeyemi won a fellowship to study West African mythology and culture in Salvador, Brazil, an experience that would later inspire Children of Blood and Bone. She moved to California and began working part time at a film production company in Los Angeles, alongside writing her first novel.

That first attempt took four and a half years to write and received 63 rejections. She decided to drop the manuscript and wrote Children of Blood and Bone instead. When it was finally published in 2018 it quickly became one of the most talked about YA novels of the year. For a writer who had spent years being turned down, the speed and scale of what followed were dizzying. “I never really adjusted, because there was so much work still to do,” she says. “It’s been 12 to 14 years of intense grinding.”

And then came the film. On paper, it was the stuff of a writer’s dreams: her novel was to be transformed into a major Hollywood production, with an impossibly starry cast including Viola Davis, Idris Elba, Regina King, Damson Idris, Amandla Stenberg and Cynthia Erivo, premiering in January 2027. Adeyemi co-wrote the screenplay, but as the adaptation progressed, she became increasingly unhappy with the process.

In July, Adeyemi posted a five-minute video on TikTok in which she described the adaptation process as “the worst thing I have ever had to live through”. She said she had left the set “hyperventilating and sobbing”, and that afterwards she experienced severe physical pain and panic attacks. “I never want to hear about this project again,” she said.

She says she had little hesitation about speaking publicly. “I understood that if I didn’t speak up, I couldn’t move forward,” she explains. “I can’t really worry about the response, because I don’t have to live with how people respond to me – I have to live with me, every day.”

When I ask what exactly happened on set, however, Adeyemi hesitates. “I won’t go into the specifics,” she says carefully. “[But] the whole journey of the trilogy and the adaptation felt biblical … It took all of me.”

There has, though, been public discussion around the film’s casting of Amandla Stenberg, who is mixed race, and questions around colourism: Stenberg’s character is described in the book as having “dark copper skin”. Adeyemi’s July TikTok also appeared to show messages she sent to Stenberg in February 2025, around the time Stenberg responded to the colourism backlash, telling the actor: “Do not ever use my name in an interview or video again. Do not text me. Do not call me.”

When I ask Adeyemi whether she wants to clarify anything about the casting, she demurs. “With a film, the director makes every decision,” she says. “With my book I can talk about every choice down to the commas, because that’s truly in my hands. So there’s nothing for me to add, other than the clarity that these aren’t my choices.”

She is clear, though, about one thing. When I ask her if she would ever adapt another one of her books for screen she responds simply: “Never.” She has no desire to watch the upcoming film either. “I still don’t plan to watch it, but it’s not really for me to watch,” she says.

Instead, she is trying to leave the world of Children of Blood and Bone behind, and focus on what she has achieved. “I’m proud of my strength, resilience, and grace,” she says.

She is also proud of what she believes her debut set in motion: the fact that she can now walk into a bookshop and see shelves of dark-skinned protagonists across fantasy, romance, thrillers and mysteries. “The girls who grew up after me will never have that experience,” she says. As her publisher told her: “You changed things.”

BreakingNewsTab.title: Andy Burnham proposes NHS-style social care system for England
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Andy Burnham wants to offer access to free social care services to everyone in England, and will put his plans before voters at the next general election.

The prime minister told the BBC that it would be a system in which "everyone contributes, everyone is covered". He did not rule out tax rises, acknowledging it may be "difficult or unpopular" with some.

Burnham said he wants to set out his "vision" on Tuesday and Whitehall troubleshooter Baroness Casey, who is conducting a review, will advise on the "best way of doing it".

Shadow home secretary Chris Philp said the PM was suggesting Labour wanted "more tax rises" to pay for the reforms, adding the Conservatives would not support this.

Burnham has made reforming social care one of his flagship policies and has spoken of the experience of his father Roy, who had Alzheimer's and died earlier this month.

While he has been clear on his ambition to make changes to the system, he has yet to explain how any changes would be funded.

Adult social care provides state support to help people live more independently, including assistance at home.

Unlike the NHS, social care is not free at the point of use. In England and Northern Ireland, people with savings worth more than £23,250 are not entitled to help with care costs from their council.

In Wales and Scotland, different rules apply in terms of eligibility.

Speaking to the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, the prime minister said: "I am talking about a system that works on NHS principles because that is the only way you can make it work.

"There is free personal care elsewhere in the UK. I don't think it's right that people in England don't get the same and it's not something we're going to rush."

Personal care offered in Scotland is available to all adults who are assessed as needing help with tasks including eating and bathing.

Burnham said the changes would have to be "done carefully, without putting extra strain on the public purse".

But he said that "nothing is off the table at this moment in time" in terms of how the proposals would be funded.

When he was told it had been estimated that a system for everyone in England that is free at the point of use could cost taxpayers £18bn a year, Burnham replied: "It's not that high."

He said people already face a "huge cost" at the moment and that social care in England is "as unfair as American healthcare, where the most vulnerable in society can lose everything, they can be wiped out".

Burnham added there is also a cost to the NHS due to the "huge number" of people in hospitals across England who cannot be discharged home "because the social care isn't there".

Asked whether everyone will have to contribute to his proposed system, Burnham replied: "It will be a system of that kind – so everyone contributes, everyone is covered but not precisely necessarily in the same way that we currently pay for the NHS."

He said the details developed by Baroness Casey would be subject to cross-party talks in a bid to "build consensus".

Baroness Casey was originally tasked by former PM Sir Keir Starmer to deliver her review of social care in 2028, but Burnham asked her to bring that forward to next summer.

On the timeline, Burnham added: "I'm going to say that we stick to the manifesto because I have to keep people's trust, and there are commitments in the manifesto that would make it hard to do in this Parliament."

The Labour manifesto in 2024 made clear commitments on tax, including not to increase national insurance, income tax or VAT.

Burnham added: "I don't think you can reform this system without consensus. I will develop a very clear plan and I will put that plan to the public at a general election and that will be where the plan gets tested and people will then be able to decide."

Philp said tax increases would be a "red line" for the Conservatives and they would "not under any circumstances" support more of them.

He said the country is "already taxed too highly", telling the BBC: "If more money is needed, for example, for social care or indeed for defence we would find that money through savings elsewhere, particularly in the welfare budget."

Labour MP Darren Jones, who served as a cabinet minister in Sir Keir's government, said Burnham was being "very bold and brave" on social care.

He said: "Politics is about prioritisation and these things do cost money and so we'll need to see the detail of that policy."

He told Laura Kuenssberg that scrapping the pensions triple lock was an "option that the government should consider alongside others" in order to fund social care reforms.

The triple lock pension policy guarantees that the state pension will increase by either average wage growth, inflation or 2.5% - whichever is highest.

Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said Burnham can show he is "serious about fixing care" by getting on with the cross-party talks that began in July.

He added: "This can't just be a series of No 10 headlines with no real action."

Reform UK's economic spokesman Robert Jenrick said: "Andy Burnham refuses to rule out his universal death tax.

"He's too weak to cut the benefits bill so he's coming for your home instead."

Burnham accused previous generations of politicians of "cowardice" for failing to reform social care, although his push for change is not without jeopardy.

He previously produced a plan for a national care service while serving as health secretary in Gordon Brown's Labour government.

It was suggested this would be paid for through a compulsory contribution, including from people's estates after they had died.

The idea was branded a "death tax" by Labour's opponents and the proposals went no further after the party lost the 2010 general election.

At the 2017 general election, then-Conservative Prime Minister Theresa May was accused of trying to introduce a "dementia tax" by proposing that people receiving care at home pay for the full costs if they were worth at least £100,000.

The policy sparked a political outcry and the Conservatives lost their majority in the House of Commons at the election.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Orange Order march row goes to heart of ongoing divisions in Northern Ireland
BreakingNewsTab.text:
History shows that when the politics of Northern Ireland are wrapped up in a street dispute, friction is seldom far away.

Bitter rows in the Stormont chamber between unionists and nationalists happen almost every week, but ground-level arguments are rare these days.

The Drumcree parade dispute in Portadown is a clash of political cultures.

The Orange Order is a Protestant pro-British organisation. The area where it wants to walk is largely Catholic, and predominantly inhabited by pro-Irish nationalists.

This dispute over a piece of road is not just a local problem. It has the potential to affect other parts of Northern Ireland and the power-sharing arrangements at Stormont.

"What happens at Drumcree never stays at Drumcree," was how one retired politician put it.

When the parade dispute first erupted into violence in the mid-1990s, the disorder spread to other places - and almost derailed the peace process.

But while it was never fully resolved, the dispute faded over the next 30 years. Its sudden re-emergence has caught most people by surprise, including many politicians.

What happened was that a legal case was brought to court over the dispute early this summer, re-opening the debate.

The two largest parties in Northern Ireland, Sinn Féin and the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP), have been on opposite sides of the argument.

Sinn Féin are firmly behind the residents. The DUP fully supports the Orange Order.

They may be partners in the devolved government at Stormont, but when it comes to Drumcree they could not be further apart.

As always in Northern Ireland, the historical context is important.

Although there has been an uneasy calm in Portadown over the parading issue in recent years, the Orange Order regards the march as unfinished business.

In 1998, it was banned from completing its Drumcree march - which includes the Garvaghy Road - and has been repeatedly refused permission to finish the route ever since.

It has applied and been turned down more than 1,000 times in the past three decades.

It says it is being denied a traditional walk which dates back to the early 1800s.

A Parades Commission was set up in the late 1990s to adjudicate on marching disputes and, until now, it has consistently ruled against the route.

The Orange Order's legal challenge to a ruling in June this year succeeded on procedural grounds.

The order subsequently re-applied for permission to carry out the parade, albeit a scaled-back version with only 35 participants rather than 400 - and was successful.

Nationalist residents on the Garvaghy Road were left shocked and angry.

For them, the parade is triumphalist and unwelcome in the area.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Suffolk and Essex NHS remove 10 staff over Noah Woods data breach
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Ten NHS staff have been removed from duty or suspended after a data breach involving the digital medical records of three-year-old Noah Woods.

Launching an "urgent" investigation, Dr Martin Mansfield, deputy chief medical officer at East Suffolk and North Essex NHS Foundation Trust, said that any unauthorised access of patient data was "completely unacceptable".

The trust has apologised "unreservedly" to Noah's family and said disciplinary action would be taken if needed.

A major search for Noah was carried out in the village of Brantham, Suffolk, after the child went missing on 15 September. His body was found the next day in a nearby pond by police divers.

A spokesperson for the trust said 10 employees had been "removed from active duty or suspended whilst investigations are concluded".

It comes after Sir Jim Mackey, the chief executive of NHS England, wrote to every trust on Friday, ordering stronger measures to tackle data breaches.

"We have seen too many cases of people abusing that trust, and enough is enough," said Sir Jim.

"Anyone who thinks they can satisfy their curiosity by looking at a patient's record should know this: they will be found out, they may lose their career and could end up with a criminal record."

At least 1,300 people helped in the search for Noah in the 24 hours before he was found.

A tribute issued by his family called him a "happy, cheeky, playful" boy who loved to laugh. His mother urged other parents to "hold their children a little tighter and cherish every moment".

An inquest, which opened on Friday, heard that the three-year-old had left a play area "through a gap in the fence".

Assistant coroner Jyoti Gill said it was a "very sad and tragic death" as she opened and adjourned the inquest in Ipswich.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Two mass shootings in South Africa leave 27 dead
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Twenty-seven people have been killed in two mass shootings hours apart in South Africa, the latest gun violence to hit the country.

Seventeen people were killed when eight gunmen stormed a bar close to Johannesburg on Saturday evening, with 15 more injured.

In a separate shooting in the early hours of Sunday morning, 10 people were killed outside an entertainment venue in a township near Cape Town and a further 11 were injured.

South Africa has one of the highest murder rates in the world and has struggled to contain gang-related gun violence in recent years. Police have not given a definitive motive for either of the latest attacks.

In Johannesburg, gunmen opened fire on customers outside the bar before continuing the attack inside and torching two vehicles before fleeing.

Police said thirteen men and four women were killed.

Gauteng Police Commissioner Lt Gen Tommy Mthombeni said people from Ethiopia and Lesotho were among those caught up in the shooting, but that the vast majority were South African.

He also said police believed the motive behind the shooting was robbery, as personal belongings had been taken, but that they could not rule out turf wars between illegal mining groups.

Mining without permission in abandoned shafts or dump sites is a persistent problem in South Africa, causing numerous deaths from unsafe conditions. Authorities say the miners are typically undocumented migrants recruited by organised crime gangs.

Earlier, deputy provincial police commissioner Maj Gen Fred Kekana said the attack may have been a retaliation for an incident last month, in which one person was killed and another wounded, according to news agency AFP.

He said at the scene that police had clear pictures and in some cases names for the suspects.

In Cape Town, five victims died at the scene and a further five people died in hospital.

No arrests had been made in either case on Sunday morning.

The two mass shootings came days after 11 people were killed in the city of Durban when gunmen stormed a house in the KwaMakhutha township.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Iranian minister says only negotiation can end conflict after Trump rejects Hormuz deal
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Only a "negotiated solution" can end the conflict between the US and Iran, Tehran's foreign minister has said, after President Donald Trump publicly rejected a proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

Trump told reporters at the White House that Iran's proposal was not "acceptable" and that Tehran wanted to make a deal to open the strait to commercial shipping within seven days because "they're losing so badly".

In a post on Telegram, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi acknowledged Trump's rejection, but said Iran would wait for a "definitive" official US response.

He said the president had made contradictory statements in the past.

Araghchi said the conditions to open the strait were the same that had been included in a memorandum of understanding (MOU) between the US and Iran that was signed in June.

Iran said it had raised reopening the strait and ending hostilities during negotiations on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York this past week.

The vital waterway through which around a fifth of the world's gas and oil supply usually flows has been effectively closed since the outbreak of war in February.

"I'm rejecting their deal," Trump said on Saturday, adding that the US already had "total control" of the strait, with "massive amounts of oil" passing through it, causing massive rises in global oil prices and steep fuel cost increases for consumers.

Araghchi wrote on Telegram that Trump "has made many good statements, as well as many contradictory ones, which unfortunately we hear frequently".

He continued: "We are waiting for the mediators to convey the definitive views to us, and we will make a decision based on them."

Separately, Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian, who travelled to New York for the UN general assembly, told the BBC's US news partner CBS that "distrust created by this war needs to be overcome" in order for talks to be successful.

He said the Iranians were open to talks on implementing the MOU in stages in order to end the impasse, but that the "US needs to show it does not intend to overthrow our government".

Pezeshkian said Trump had "tore up" the MOU when the US resumed its bombing campaign, adding: "If we don't abide by what we have written down, can we really resolve it by dialogue?"

He was also asked about Iran's new Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, who was injured in the US strike which killed his father in February and has not been seen in public since. Reports have claimed he suffered serious injuries to his legs and face.

Pezeshkian said he had met the supreme leader on two occasions, telling CBS he had "no specific ongoing health issues or challenges" and had been well enough to hold seven hours of talks.

Oman, which has been acting as a mediator between the US and Iran, called for all parties to continue having open dialogue to resolve the crisis.

Oman's foreign minister, Sayyid Badr bin Hamad bin Hamood Albusaidi, told the UN General Debate that "all parties" should cooperate with Oman in efforts to safeguard navigation in the strategic waterway.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Venezuela releases dozens of political prisoners as election calls grow
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Venezuelan authorities have released a slew of political prisoners, human rights groups say, days after the nation's interim leader met US President Donald Trump in New York.

Among those released in the early hours of Saturday morning was Wilder Vasquez, who was handed a five-year sentence in 2018 over claims he was plotting to kill former President Nicolás Maduro.

Opposition figures have renewed calls for free elections after interim President Delcy Rodriguez held talks with Trump, who captured Maduro earlier this year, at the UN General Assembly on Tuesday.

Her administration previously released hundreds of prisoners as part of a reconciliation effort following Maduro's seizure.

However, these releases slowed to a trickle in April after Rodriguez said the scheme was "coming to an end".

Venezuela's government has not made any statement concerning the latest releases, nor has it indicated whether they were the result of her conversation with the US president.

Gonzalo Himiob, vice-president of rights group Foro Penal, said "a significant number" of political prisoners had been released on Saturday morning from several of Venezuela's detention centres.

Foro Penal confirmed the release of Miguel Castillo Cedeño, who it said had been arbitrarily detained since June 2019.

Also released was Frank Cabañas, who rights groups say had been held in prison for nine years after being linked to the death of a police officer. Foro Penal said he was the only suspect who remained detained, despite family members reporting that he was suffering health problems last year.

Opposition and human rights groups have said Maduro's government used the detention of political prisoners to stamp out dissent and silence critics for years.

Rodriguez has sought to frame her interim government as more permissive of political dissent while currying favour with the US. The prisoner release scheme was a key concession by her administration to the US.

However, her decision to end the scheme attracted criticism from opposition and rights groups. Foro Penal said it was stopped with less than half of the nation's political prisoners released.

Rodriguez's government continues to deny dissidents are jailed. It has cast the release of prisoners as a gesture of goodwill and reconciliation.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Time running out for Tennessee killer Christa Pike who says she's too damaged for death row
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Ashlee Sellars last heard from her friend Christa Pike earlier this week, when Pike texted her from her cell on death row as she prepares to be killed by lethal injection by the US state of Tennessee.

Pike told Sellars she does not want any of her loved ones to be present on Wednesday when she is executed.

"She doesn't want us to experience that," Sellars says.

Sellars finds it hard to reconcile this woman, whom she has only known to be kind and protective, with the person who committed a heinous crime 31 years ago.

Pike, now 50, was 18 when she and her boyfriend at the time, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and murdered Colleen Slemmer, a 19-year-old they met at a job training camp for troubled teens.

The murder created a media frenzy in Knoxville, Tennessee in 1995 when Colleen was found with a pentagram, a symbol of Satanic ritual, carved into her chest.

Pike had accused Colleen of insulting her and trying to steal her boyfriend. Two other residents at the camp later testified that Pike had bragged about the murder before and after, and showed them a piece of Colleen's skull.

A year later she was sentenced to death, while Shipp - who was 17 at the time - was given a life sentence with the possibility of parole.

Now, after years of failed appeals, Pike's execution has been set for Wednesday. If it goes ahead, she will be the first woman put to death in Tennessee in more than 200 years. Only 18 women have been executed in the US since the 1970s, compared to 1,663 men.

Colleen's mother has said she wants Pike's execution to happen so that her daughter "finally can be resting".

But Pike's lawyers, who filed a 226-page clemency petition, are still hoping for a last-minute reprieve, and UN human rights experts have also called for the execution to be stopped., external

Pike has a documented history of childhood sexual abuse, abandonment and neglect. Her lawyers believe that if she was found guilty of the same crime today as a teenager she would not receive a death sentence.

In the years since her sentencing, her defence team have uncovered details about her childhood that they say the jury never had the chance to consider.

"It is mind-boggling that they did not present any of her history of abuse and rape, even though they knew about it," says Sandra Babcock, an expert in gender and the death penalty at Cornell Law School, who has worked on Pike's defence.

"Her case is so uniquely compelling, not just because of her really incomprehensible history of sexual violence but the combination of that with her youth and her mental illness."

In 1995, forensic psychologist Dr Diana McCoy was hired by Pike's defence team and found she was severely neglected by both of her parents. McCoy's report found Pike was physically and sexually abused by several of her mother's husbands and boyfriends, and raped several times, once when she was 11 and again aged 17. Later it was discovered that she was repeatedly raped as a toddler by her grandmother's boyfriend. McCoy said Pike's mother didn't believe her that these rapes happened.

But Pike's trial lawyer did not put McCoy on the stand or call many of the witnesses she recommended. These details emerged more than a decade later in a court hearing reviewing her case, when a new team of lawyers claimed ineffective assistance of counsel, a claim that was denied by the judge.

In 2021 Pike was diagnosed with bipolar disorder in prison and has been medicated since.

Later, another forensic psychologist working for Pike's defence, Dr Bethany Brand, who assessed Pike in 2023, said her case was extremely rare because she was abused by so many people who should have protected her.

"Her childhood was replete with physical, sexual, and emotional abuse. She was sexually violated by a number of men, starting before she was school age," she says.

Brand says Pike had untreated manic episodes due to bipolar disorder and untreated PTSD. "Both of those things together absolutely influenced how threatened she felt by the girl she ended up killing and her lack of emotional control in that situation."

Babcock adds: "If they let her be executed, then what it tells us is that the death penalty in this country is just a joke. It's not for the worst of the worst. It is for the people who receive the worst legal representation and who are the most damaged and vulnerable."

Last year, Tennessee's Supreme Court ruled Pike had not shown circumstances that would justify commuting her sentence. Her appeals process had been exhausted and a date was set for her execution.

A federal appeals court had earlier ruled that the jury had already heard about her difficult childhood during testimony from her mother, father, and aunt during her trial. And that new evidence of bipolar disorder, PTSD, and brain damage "mostly repeated" what the jury had heard and would not have changed the verdict.

The row has some parallels with the high-profile case of murderer Lisa Montgomery, whose lawyers also argued she was a mentally ill victim of abuse who deserved mercy.

Montgomery's legal challenges failed to commute her sentence, and she was executed by lethal injection in Indiana in 2021.

Unless she is granted clemency by Tennessee Governor Bill Lee, Pike will be executed on 30 September. That decision is unlikely to come until the last moment, and Lee has never granted clemency in a death penalty case before.

The Tennessee Supreme Court this week denied Pike's request to halt the execution. Her counsel say they have been discussing next steps.

On her execution day, Pike has requested an all-female team. She says being held down by a group of men will exacerbate her trauma. The state of Tennessee has said the goal is that female guards will transfer Pike to the prison where she will be executed but hasn't guaranteed it.

Colleen's mother May Martinez supports Christa's execution.

"She did the crime. I think she should pay for it," she said on Knoxville TV station WBIR in 2021, and told the BBC this week she still stands by those comments.

Pike should suffer before she dies, Martinez told WBIR. "I would feel better that she felt the same pain that Colleen did."

"My heart breaks every single day because I keep reliving it and reliving it, and I can't no more, and I want this to happen before I die," she added.

"There's not a day goes by that I don't think about Colleen or how she died and how rough it was. I just want Christa down so I can end it, relieve my daughter, so she finally can be resting."

The Justice Coalition, a victims' rights advocacy group, has raised money to help Martinez travel to Tennessee to watch the execution.

The group's executive director, Robert Bracewell, said this sentence was determined by a jury of Pike's peers and it is what Colleen's family want.

"We stand firm with the family that on the 30 September her execution ought to proceed."

Ashlee Sellars grapples with two seemingly conflicting beliefs: that Colleen's mother has a right to feel justice has been served and that everyone, including her friend Christa, deserves a chance at redemption.

"When I think about reconciling who you see on TV or the horrible tragedy that happened with Colleen, the only thing that makes sense to me is around mental health and trauma and the way that people process stuff in a moment when they don't have the things that they need," Sellars says.

"These horrible things happen in your youth and then those traumas moved through you, in our community, and you cause harm to somebody else."

Sellars met Pike in prison while serving a 25-year sentence for her involvement in a robbery-murder. They spoke to each other through the meal flaps in their doors on the high security unit. Now, Sellars works as an advocate for justice reform and victims of crime.

"People want to know that everyone's life matters, right? They want to know that Colleen's life mattered," she says.

"Christa in this moment, I think she is fighting much more for her life to matter than she is to actually live."
